11:["$","h2",null,{"className":"text-[15px] font-bold uppercase tracking-wide text-ink mt-10 pt-6 border-t border-hairline","children":"HSB Tuning: Hue First, Then Saturation, Then Brightness"}]
12:["$","p",null,{"className":"mt-4 text-[15px] leading-[1.75] text-ink","children":"Every how-to-play guide for this genre tells you to set hue first. Few explain why, so here is the lab version."}]
13:["$","p",null,{"className":"mt-4 text-[15px] leading-[1.75] text-ink","children":[["$","strong",null,{"children":"Hue is categorical; saturation and brightness are relative."}]," Saturation and brightness only mean something once a hue family is fixed — \"60% saturation of the wrong hue\" is still the wrong color. Get the hue slider into the right neighborhood first (±10° is close enough to refine), then use saturation to control how far the color sits from gray, then brightness to place it on the light–dark axis. Working in that order means each slider answers one perceptual question instead of three at once."]}]
14:["$","p",null,{"className":"mt-4 text-[15px] leading-[1.75] text-ink","children":[["$","strong",null,{"children":"Why pastels are harder than they look."}]," Low-saturation colors compress your margin for error. In a vivid red, being 8° off in hue is a modest shift; in a pale, washed-out tint, the eye is far more sensitive to small hue and chroma moves — and CIEDE2000 knows it. The formula's weighting terms make tiny differences count more in low-chroma regions, exactly where human vision is most discriminating. So when the proof looks like \"barely pink paper,\" slow down: pastel rounds punish sloppy hue work harder than saturated ones."]}]
15:["$","p",null,{"className":"mt-4 text-[15px] leading-[1.75] text-ink","children":[["$","strong",null,{"children":"Your screen is part of the test."}]," The arithmetic runs on RGB values, but your eye judges through your display and your room. Keep screen brightness steady across rounds, switch off night-shift and warm color filters while you play, and avoid judging a proof next to a sunlit window. A display that drifts warmer over the evening won't change the numbers — it will change your readings of them."]}]
